nodes.body:
# Multi-Harness Agent Platform â€” Full Architecture & Implementation Plan

## 1. Vision

Build a multi-tenant platform that allows users to:

- Discover and install multiple AI agent harnesses.
- Pin and manage harness versions and immutable runtime artifacts.
- Start many concurrent sessions across different harnesses.
- Run different harnesses simultaneously for different tasks.
- Select models independently from harnesses and providers.
- Connect MCP servers and manage short-lived OAuth/access tokens.
- Surface native harness commands, capabilities, notifications, compaction, memory, plugins, and extensions through a dynamic UI.
- Persist conversations, session state, memory, workspaces, artifacts, and checkpoints.
- Run untrusted/long-running agents in isolated runtimes.
- Track usage, cost, audit events, approvals, and operational health.
- Add new harnesses through a stable adapter SDK and conformance test suite.

The core architectural principle is:

> Normalize the platform-level lifecycle and security model, but do not force every harness into the same internal implementation.

---

# 2. Supported Harnesses

Initial catalog:

- [Pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) â€” Minimal and highly extensible agent harness with an agent runtime, tools, sessions, and a coding-agent CLI.
- [OpenHarness](https://github.com/hotsun/openharness) â€” Open-source agent harness focused on tools, skills, memory, plugins, permissions, and multi-agent workflows.
- [jcode](https://github.com/Ravi-bit-app/jcode) â€” Coding-agent harness designed around efficient multi-session workflows and extensibility.
- [Grok CLI](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-cli) â€” General-purpose terminal agent from xAI for coding and agentic workflows.
- [OpenCode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) â€” Open-source terminal coding agent with an extensible architecture and support for multiple model providers.
- [Goose](https://github.com/block/goose) â€” Extensible open-source agent with tools, extensions, and MCP integration.
- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) â€” Autonomous software-development platform providing agents with coding, terminal, browser, and task-execution capabilities.
- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) â€” Agent framework focused on autonomously solving software-engineering tasks and GitHub issues.
- [OpenAI Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) â€” Open-source terminal coding agent with sandboxed execution and tool-driven workflows.
- [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) â€” Open-source terminal agent for coding and general agentic tasks with tools and extensibility.
- [Cline](https://github.com/cline/cline) â€” IDE-based autonomous coding agent supporting tool execution, MCP, browser interaction, and human-in-the-loop workflows.
- [Roo Code](https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code) â€” Extensible coding-agent environment supporting custom modes, MCP, instructions, and autonomous execution.
- [Aider](https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider) â€” Terminal-based AI pair-programming agent with repository-aware context, code editing, and command execution.
- [Open Harness](https://github.com/MaxGfeller/open-harness) â€” Code-first SDK for building composable AI agents with sessions, tools, middleware, and model providers.
- [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) â€” Open-source agent harness by DeepSeek AI built around a plugin-based architecture.

> Verify current upstream APIs, licenses, release artifacts, and runtime requirements before production integration.

---

# 3. Core Architectural Principles

## 3.1 Harness != Model != Provider != Credential != Runtime

Keep these independent:

```text
Harness
  |
  +-- Harness Version
  |
  +-- Adapter Version
  |
  +-- Runtime Artifact
  |
  +-- Model Configuration
        |
        +-- Provider
        |
        +-- Credential
```

## 3.2 Control Plane vs Data Plane

### Control Plane

Responsible for:

- Identity
- Tenants
- Users and teams
- Projects
- Harness registry
- Versions
- Installation configuration
- Model registry
- Policies
- Scheduling
- Quotas
- Billing
- Session metadata
- Configuration
- Audit

### Data Plane

Responsible for:

- Runtime containers/VMs
- Harness processes
- MCP calls
- Tool execution
- Workspace access
- Agent execution
- Streaming events
- Artifacts

This separation is essential for scaling.

## 3.3 Immutable execution

Never run a production session from `latest`.

Resolve:

```text
harness + version
        |
        v
immutable artifact digest
```

Every execution stores the exact digest.

---

# 4. High-Level Architecture

```text
                             +----------------------+
                             |       Web UI         |
                             | Dynamic UI Renderer  |
                             +----------+-----------+
                                        |
                                 REST + WebSocket
                                        |
                             +----------v-----------+
                             |     API Gateway      |
                             +----------+-----------+
                                        |
                 +----------------------+----------------------+
                 |                      |                      |
                 v                      v                      v
          Identity/RBAC          Conversation Manager     Billing/Usage
                 |                      |
                 +-----------+----------+
                             |
                             v
                    Task Orchestrator
                             |
                    Capability Broker
                             |
          +------------------+------------------+
          |                  |                  |
          v                  v                  v
      Harnesses            Plugins             MCP
          |                  |                  |
      Adapters         Plugin Runtime       MCP Gateway
          |                                      |
          v                                      v
    Runtime Manager                       Credential Manager
          |
          v
  Containers / VMs / K8s
          |
          v
    Harness Process
          |
          v
    Event Normalizer
          |
          v
       Event Bus
          |
    +-----+------+----------+----------+
    |            |          |          |
    v            v          v          v
  State        Memory    Artifacts  Observability
  Store
```

---

# 5. Major Platform Subsystems

1. Identity & Multi-Tenancy
2. API Gateway
3. Project/Conversation Manager
4. Task Orchestrator
5. Harness Registry
6. Harness Version/Artifact Manager
7. Harness Adapter Layer
8. Runtime Manager
9. Distributed Scheduler
10. Model Registry
11. Model Resolver
12. Model Gateway
13. MCP Gateway
14. Credential/Secrets Manager
15. Plugin Manager
16. Tool Permission Engine
17. Workspace Manager
18. Memory Manager
19. Session State Manager
20. Checkpoint/Recovery Manager
21. Event Bus
22. Notification Gateway
23. Dynamic UI Schema/Renderer
24. Artifact Manager
25. Usage/Cost Metering
26. Billing
27. Observability
28. Audit Log
29. Approval/HITL
30. Security/Sandboxing
31. Quotas/Rate Limiting
32. Feature Flags
33. Conformance Testing
34. Developer SDK
35. Disaster Recovery

---

# 6. Multi-Tenancy

Resource hierarchy:

```text
Organization
  |
  +-- Users
  +-- Teams
  +-- Projects
       |
       +-- Conversations
       |     |
       |     +-- Messages
       |
       +-- Tasks
       |     |
       |     +-- Executions
       |
       +-- Workspaces
       +-- Harness Installations
       +-- Credentials
       +-- Policies
```

Every persistent resource should carry tenant ownership.

Typical identifiers:

```text
tenant_id
user_id
team_id
project_id
conversation_id
task_id
execution_id
session_id
workspace_id
artifact_id
```

Never rely only on frontend authorization.

---

# 7. Authentication and Authorization

## Authentication

Support:

- Email/password where appropriate.
- OAuth/OIDC.
- SSO for enterprise.
- API keys.
- Service accounts.
- Short-lived access tokens.

## Authorization

Use RBAC initially:

```text
Owner
Admin
Developer
Member
Viewer
```

Then add policy-based controls for:

- Harness installation
- Model access
- MCP access
- Tool execution
- Workspace access
- Production environments
- Plugin installation
- Arbitrary container execution
- Cost limits

---

# 8. Harness Registry

The registry describes available harnesses.

Example:

```yaml
harness:
  id: pi
  name: Pi
  vendor: community

versions:
  - version: 0.9.2
    channel: stable
    status: supported

capabilities:
  sessions: true
  streaming: true
  commands: true
  mcp: true
  compaction: true
```

The registry should not contain only a list of names. It should also contain:

- Supported platforms
- Architectures
- Release channels
- Artifact metadata
- Runtime requirements
- Adapter compatibility
- Capabilities
- Configuration schema
- UI schema support
- Security requirements
- License metadata
- Health status
- Deprecation/EOL state

---

# 9. Harness Version and Binary Management

## Version hierarchy

There are independent versions:

```text
Platform Version
Harness Version
Adapter Version
Runtime Image Version
Plugin Version
MCP Protocol Version
```

Do not tie adapter version to harness version.

## Artifact model

Example:

```yaml
harness: pi
version: 0.9.2

artifact:
  type: container
  image: registry.example.com/harness/pi:0.9.2
  digest: sha256:abc123

platforms:
  - linux/amd64
  - linux/arm64
```

## Installation flow

```text
User selects harness/version
        |
        v
Version Resolver
        |
        v
Compatibility Check
        |
        v
Artifact Verification
        |
        v
Private Registry
        |
        v
Runtime Manager
```

Verify:

- SHA256 digest
- Artifact signature where available
- Source/release provenance
- License
- Security policy
- Runtime requirements

## Version channels

Support:

```text
stable
beta
nightly
```

## Version pinning

Store:

```json
{
  "harness": "pi",
  "version": "0.9.2",
  "artifact_digest": "sha256:abc123",
  "adapter_version": "2.1.0"
}
```

## Harness Lock

Projects should optionally contain:

```yaml
harnesses:
  pi:
    version: 0.9.2
    digest: sha256:abc123

  opencode:
    version: 0.8.3
    digest: sha256:def456
```

This provides reproducibility.

---

# 10. Runtime Management

Prefer containerized execution over installing all harnesses on the host.

```text
Worker Node
  |
  +-- Runtime: Pi 0.9.2
  +-- Runtime: Goose 1.2.1
  +-- Runtime: OpenCode 0.8.3
```

Runtime should support:

- Start
- Stop
- Pause where possible
- Resume
- Health checks
- Resource limits
- Network policy
- Secret injection
- Workspace mounting
- Artifact mounting
- Log collection
- Metrics
- Timeout
- Cleanup

Use a runtime abstraction so Docker/Kubernetes/VM execution can evolve independently.

---

# 11. Distributed Scheduling

At scale:

```text
API
 |
 v
Task Queue
 |
 v
Scheduler
 |
 +-- CPU availability
 +-- memory
 +-- GPU
 +-- region
 +-- tenant quota
 +-- harness/version
 +-- runtime warm pool
 +-- priority
 +-- cost
 |
 v
Worker
```

Use queues with:

- Retry
- Exponential backoff
- Dead-letter queue
- Idempotency
- Priority
- Visibility timeout
- Cancellation

---

# 12. Harness Adapter Architecture

Every harness should implement a platform adapter.

Conceptual interface:

```python
class HarnessAdapter:
    def metadata(self): ...
    def capabilities(self): ...

    def install(self): ...
    def start(self): ...
    def stop(self): ...

    def create_session(self): ...
    def resume_session(self): ...
    def terminate_session(self): ...

    def send_message(self): ...
    def stream_events(self): ...

    def list_commands(self): ...
    def execute_command(self): ...

    def list_tools(self): ...
    def configure_mcp(self): ...

    def get_state(self): ...
    def get_context(self): ...
    def compact(self): ...

    def get_memory(self): ...
    def get_plugins(self): ...

    def health(self): ...
```

The exact implementation varies by harness.

The platform owns the lifecycle contract.

---

# 13. Harness Capability Manifest

Each adapter should expose:

```json
{
  "harness": "pi",
  "version": "0.9.2",

  "capabilities": {
    "sessions": true,
    "streaming": true,
    "commands": true,
    "mcp": true,
    "plugins": true,
    "memory": true,
    "compaction": true
  }
}
```

UI should render capabilities dynamically.

Never assume all harnesses support the same features.

---

# 14. Dynamic UI Architecture

Use three UI levels.

## Level 1 â€” Universal

Examples:

- Session
- Messages
- Status
- Tools
- Events
- Runtime
- Artifacts

## Level 2 â€” Capability-based

Examples:

- Compaction
- Commands
- MCP
- Memory
- Plugins
- Skills
- Modes
- Extensions
- Recipes
- Workflows

## Level 3 â€” Harness-specific

Unique features can be rendered by optional frontend plugins.

---

# 15. Dynamic UI Component Protocol

Backend returns semantic UI components:

```json
{
  "type": "metric",
  "label": "Context Usage",
  "value": 64,
  "unit": "%"
}
```

Frontend component registry:

```text
metric    -> MetricCard
list      -> List
table     -> DataTable
form      -> DynamicForm
terminal  -> Terminal
markdown  -> Markdown
json      -> JSONViewer
progress  -> ProgressBar
timeline  -> Timeline
tree      -> TreeView
code      -> CodeViewer
```

The backend describes semantics, not exact CSS/layout.

---

# 16. Dynamic Forms

Use JSON Schema for:

- Harness configuration
- Commands
- Tool parameters
- Model parameters
- Plugin settings
- MCP configuration

Example:

```json
{
  "command": "/model",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "model": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": ["model-a", "model-b"]
      }
    },
    "required": ["model"]
  }
}
```

The UI can automatically generate a form.

---

# 17. Commands

Harnesses may expose commands such as:

```text
/help
/model
/compact
/custom-command
```

Adapter returns:

```json
{
  "commands": [
    {
      "name": "/compact",
      "type": "action"
    },
    {
      "name": "/model",
      "type": "form",
      "input_schema": {}
    }
  ]
}
```

The UI builds a dynamic command palette.

Unknown commands should still be executable through a generic command interface where policy allows.

---

# 18. Events and Notifications

Harnesses may emit different event types.

Normalize common events:

```text
session.started
session.stopped
message.created
message.delta
tool.started
tool.completed
tool.failed
approval.required
runtime.error
artifact.created
```

Preserve native events:

```json
{
  "type": "harness.event",
  "harness": "pi",
  "name": "extension.loaded",
  "data": {}
}
```

Unknown events should not break the platform.

---

# 19. Event Bus

Use an event bus between runtime and platform.

```text
Harness
  |
  v
Adapter
  |
  v
Event Normalizer
  |
  v
Event Bus
  |
  +-- Session State
  +-- UI Streaming
  +-- Notifications
  +-- Observability
  +-- Audit
  +-- Usage Meter
```

WebSocket/SSE clients subscribe through the platform, not directly to containers.

---

# 20. Session Architecture

Separate:

```text
Conversation
Task
Execution
Harness Session
Runtime
```

Example:

```text
Conversation
   |
   +-- Task A
   |     |
   |     +-- Execution 1
   |           |
   |           +-- Pi Session
   |           +-- Runtime
   |
   +-- Task B
         |
         +-- Execution 2
               |
               +-- Goose Session
               +-- Runtime
```

This allows multiple harnesses to operate simultaneously.

---

# 21. Session State

Platform-level session state:

```text
session_id
tenant_id
user_id
conversation_id
task_id
harness_id
harness_version
adapter_version
runtime_id
workspace_id
model_id
status
created_at
updated_at
```

Harness-specific state remains in the adapter/runtime where required.

Do not try to force every harness's internal state into one database schema.

---

# 22. Multiple Conversations

Use explicit identifiers:

```text
tenant
  |
  +-- user
       |
       +-- conversation
            |
            +-- messages
            +-- tasks
            +-- executions
            +-- sessions
```

Never use a single global session per user.

A user can have:

```text
Conversation A -> Pi
Conversation B -> Goose
Conversation C -> OpenCode
```

simultaneously.

---

# 23. Session Resume

Store enough platform metadata to reconnect:

```text
session_id
runtime_id
harness version
workspace
conversation
model
checkpoint
```

If the runtime is alive:

```text
Reconnect
```

If it is gone:

```text
Restore checkpoint
       |
       v
Create compatible runtime
       |
       v
Resume harness session
```

---

# 24. MCP Architecture

Do not allow every harness to independently manage credentials.

Recommended:

```text
Harness
   |
   v
Platform MCP Gateway
   |
   +-- Tool Registry
   +-- Credential Manager
   +-- OAuth Manager
   +-- Policy Engine
   +-- Rate Limiter
   +-- Audit
   |
   v
MCP Server
```

Where native harness MCP behavior is required, the adapter can bridge it.

---

# 25. Short-Lived MCP Tokens

For a 5-minute token:

```text
Session
  |
  v
MCP Gateway
  |
  v
Token Cache
  |
  +-- valid -> use
  |
  +-- near expiry -> refresh
  |
  +-- expired -> refresh
  |
  v
MCP Server
```

Never store only a token expiry and hope the harness handles it.

Use:

```text
access_token
expires_at
refresh_token / refresh mechanism
provider
scope
credential_id
```

Token refresh should happen centrally when possible.

## Important

Use a safety margin, for example:

```text
expires_at - current_time < refresh_window
```

instead of waiting for the exact expiration second.

## Concurrent refresh protection

If 20 tool calls notice an expired token simultaneously:

```text
20 requests
    |
    v
single-flight refresh
    |
    v
new token
    |
    v
20 requests continue
```

Avoid a refresh storm.

---

# 26. Model Architecture

Keep:

```text
Model
Provider
Credential
Gateway
Harness
```

independent.

## Model Registry

Store:

```text
model_id
provider
context_length
capabilities
modalities
tool_calling
reasoning
pricing
availability
```

## Model Resolver

Input:

```text
user preference
task requirements
tenant policy
model availability
cost
capabilities
```

Output:

```text
resolved model
provider
routing mode
credential reference
```

---

# 27. Model Routing Modes

Support:

```text
platform gateway
harness native
direct provider
```

Platform gateway can provide:

- Central credentials
- Routing
- Fallback
- Rate limits
- Cost tracking
- Provider abstraction
- Usage metering

Do not force native harness integrations through the gateway if that would break important functionality.

---

# 28. Model Selection Levels

Allow defaults at multiple levels:

```text
Organization
   |
Project
   |
Task
   |
Execution
```

Most specific setting wins.

Example:

```text
Organization -> Auto
Project -> Claude
Task -> GPT
Execution -> Gemini
```

---

# 29. Automatic Model Selection

Optional:

```text
Model = Auto
```

Pipeline:

```text
Task
 |
 v
Requirement extraction
 |
 v
Capability matching
 |
 v
Policy check
 |
 v
Cost/latency ranking
 |
 v
Model selection
```

Examples:

```text
Simple task -> inexpensive model
Complex reasoning -> reasoning model
Vision -> multimodal model
Large repository -> long-context model
```

---

# 30. Model Fallback

Define fallback chains:

```yaml
fallback:
  - model-a
  - model-b
  - model-c
```

Fallback should occur at safe execution boundaries.

Do not blindly switch models in the middle of a critical tool call.

---

# 31. Plugins

Separate plugin types:

```text
Platform Plugin
Harness Plugin
UI Plugin
MCP Server
Tool Plugin
Provider Plugin
```

Maintain a plugin manifest:

```yaml
plugin:
  id: github-tools
  version: 1.2.0

requires:
  platform: ">=4.0"

permissions:
  - network
  - repository.read
```

Plugin installation should include:

- Signature verification
- Version resolution
- Permission review
- Compatibility check
- Sandbox policy
- Lifecycle management
- Rollback
- Audit

---

# 32. Memory Architecture

Do not make harness memory the only memory.

Use layers:

```text
Platform Memory
  |
  +-- User memory
  +-- Project memory
  +-- Conversation memory
  +-- Task memory
  +-- Execution memory
```

And optionally:

```text
Harness Native Memory
```

Platform memory is portable across harnesses.

Harness-native memory can preserve harness-specific behavior.

## Memory types

```text
Short-term context
Conversation history
Summaries
Semantic memory
Project facts
User preferences
Task state
Artifacts/references
```

---

# 33. Compaction

Harnesses may have their own compaction mechanisms.

Treat them as capabilities:

```text
platform.compaction
harness.compaction
```

Use native compaction when it is more accurate for that harness.

Platform-level compaction can provide fallback or cross-harness summarization.

Do not overwrite harness-native state unexpectedly.

---

# 34. Workspace Manager

Every execution should have a workspace abstraction.

```text
Workspace
 |
 +-- Git repository
 +-- branch
 +-- files
 +-- dependencies
 +-- environment
 +-- snapshots
 +-- artifacts
```

Workspace modes:

```text
ephemeral
persistent
shared
snapshot
clone
```

Workspace lifecycle:

```text
create
mount
snapshot
restore
clone
destroy
```

---

# 35. Checkpoints and Recovery

Checkpoint should capture:

```text
conversation state
session metadata
workspace snapshot/reference
harness state where possible
model configuration
pending task state
```

Flow:

```text
Execution
   |
   +-- checkpoint
   +-- checkpoint
   +-- checkpoint
   |
   v
Failure
   |
   v
Restore
   |
   v
Resume
```

This is critical for long-running agents.

---

# 36. Artifacts

Agents can produce:

```text
files
patches
screenshots
logs
reports
archives
builds
videos
```

Use object storage.

Metadata:

```text
artifact_id
tenant_id
project_id
execution_id
workspace_id
type
size
checksum
storage_uri
created_at
```

---

# 37. Human-in-the-Loop

Central approval service:

```text
Agent
 |
 v
Risk Evaluation
 |
 +-- low risk -> execute
 |
 +-- high risk -> approval
                       |
                 +-----+-----+
                 v           v
              approve      reject
```

Examples requiring approval:

- Production deployment
- Database deletion
- External write
- Git push
- Secrets access
- Destructive filesystem operations

Approval should be platform-enforced, not only UI-enforced.

---

# 38. Tool Permission Engine

Assign risk:

```text
filesystem.read   LOW
git.diff           LOW
terminal           MEDIUM
git.push           HIGH
deploy             HIGH
database.delete    CRITICAL
```

Policies can depend on:

```text
tenant
user
project
workspace
environment
tool
MCP server
harness
model
```

---

# 39. Network Isolation

Runtime sandbox:

```text
Container
 |
 +-- CPU limit
 +-- memory limit
 +-- process limit
 +-- filesystem sandbox
 +-- network policy
 +-- timeout
 +-- secret policy
```

Default-deny network where practical.

Allow only approved destinations.

---

# 40. Resource Quotas

Per tenant/user/project:

```text
concurrent sessions
CPU
RAM
GPU
runtime duration
tokens
MCP calls
tool calls
storage
network
```

Example:

```text
Free:
  2 sessions
  2 CPU
  4 GB RAM

Pro:
  20 sessions
  8 CPU
  32 GB RAM

Enterprise:
  custom
```

---

# 41. Rate Limiting

Apply limits at:

```text
user
tenant
API key
project
session
harness
MCP server
model
```

Use distributed rate limiting for horizontally scaled API servers.

---

# 42. Usage and Billing

Meter:

```text
model input tokens
model output tokens
model cost
CPU seconds
memory
GPU
runtime duration
MCP calls
tool calls
storage
network
```

Store usage against:

```text
tenant
project
task
execution
session
model
harness
```

This makes future billing possible.

---

# 43. Observability

Collect:

### Logs

```text
API
scheduler
runtime
adapter
harness
MCP
model gateway
```

### Metrics

```text
active sessions
queue latency
runtime startup latency
tool latency
MCP errors
model latency
token usage
container failures
```

### Traces

Trace:

```text
user request
 -> task
 -> execution
 -> model call
 -> tool call
 -> MCP
 -> runtime
```

Use correlation IDs.

---

# 44. Audit Log

Separate security audit from normal logs.

Record:

```text
who
tenant
when
action
resource
harness
version
model
tool
MCP
approval
result
```

Examples:

```text
User installed Pi 0.9.2
User started execution
Agent called github.create_pr
Admin approved deployment
Credential was refreshed
```

Audit records should be append-only where practical.

---

# 45. Idempotency

Use idempotency keys for operations such as:

```text
create task
create session
execute tool
start runtime
install harness
```

This prevents duplicate work when clients retry.

---

# 46. Cancellation

# 69. Critical Design Rules

1. **Never depend on `latest` for production execution.**
2. **Never expose arbitrary harness containers directly to users.**

4. **Keep model/provider/credential/harness/runtime independent.**
5. **Use adapters as the compatibility boundary.**
6. **Use capability discovery instead of hardcoded feature assumptions.**
7. **Use schema-driven UI for dynamic commands/tools/configuration.**
8. **Centralize MCP credentials and token refresh where possible.**
9. **Store immutable execution metadata.**

11. **Make workspace and checkpoint recovery first-class.**

             Gateway             |             |

---

# 71. Success Criteria

The architecture is successful when you can add a new harness by doing approximately:

```text
1. Build adapter
2. Define capabilities
3. Define configuration schema
4. Package verified runtime
5. Run conformance tests
6. Register version
7. Publish
```

without modifying:

```text
authentication
sessions
MCP
model gateway
billing
workspace
memory
scheduler
UI core
```

That is the central extensibility goal.

---

# 72. Final Architecture Philosophy

The platform should behave like an **orchestration layer for heterogeneous agent runtimes**, not like a giant wrapper that tries to rewrite every harness.

The platform owns:

```text
identity
tenancy
security
policy
sessions
tasks
models
credentials
MCP
workspaces
artifacts
events
usage
observability
UI protocol
```

The harness owns:

```text
agent loop
native reasoning/context behavior
native commands
native compaction
native plugins
native extensions
native memory
native workflow semantics
```

The adapter connects the two worlds.

That boundary is what allows the platform to scale from the initial 15 harnesses to many more without turning the codebase into a collection of special cases.

nodes.title: Retrieval roadmap: alternatives to BM25, and whether hybrid + reranking is worth it here
nodes.body:
[docs/RETRIEVAL.md](https://github.com/prasadtalasila/chitragupta/blob/main/docs/RETRIEVAL.md) settles what BM25 and the embedding index each *are*, and states plainly that they are alternatives: "Nothing in this repository fuses or re-ranks the two -- there is no hybrid search here. A skill uses one or the other."

This is a write-up of what the alternatives to BM25 actually look like in Python, what a hybrid pipeline would consist of, and how much of one this repository already has. It is a proposal for discussion, not a plan of record. Nothing here is a bug report: everything it describes is documented, deliberate behaviour.

Against `main` at `d299eb4`.

---

## 1. What "an alternative to BM25" can mean

Two different things, worth separating before comparing anything:

**A different lexical scorer** -- query-likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing, DFR/PL2, or the BM25 variants (BM25+, BM25L, BM25F for multi-field). PyTerrier exposes all of these. Honestly: almost nobody switches for quality reasons. Differences on typical corpora are small and inconsistent, and default-parameter BM25 is a hard baseline. If the problem is "BM25 isn't finding the right paper", a different weighting formula is not the fix.

**A different retrieval paradigm** -- dense, learned-sparse, late-interaction, or hybrid-plus-rerank. This is where the real gains are, and it is what the rest of this covers.

## 2. The Python landscape, sorted by what it costs to adopt

Sorted by dependency and runtime cost, because that is the axis that actually decides anything here -- this project deliberately keeps the corpus layer stdlib-only.

### Zero new dependencies

- **SQLite FTS5.** Ships in most CPython `sqlite3` builds (verified available on this machine: SQLite 3.46.1). A real inverted index with a built-in `bm25()` ranking function, `MATCH` syntax with phrase/prefix/NEAR operators, and `snippet()`/`highlight()`. Same algorithm as what `src/retrieval.py` hand-rolls, but the index lives in the database and incremental update is `INSERT`/`DELETE`. Relevant here because `content/ledger.sqlite` already exists and FTS5 would subsume the bespoke `content/retrieval_index.json` fingerprint cache. Caveat: FTS5 is a compile-time option, so a stripped SQLite on some CI leg would need a fallback path -- which is a real cost against a cache that currently works.
- **DuckDB FTS.** Same idea for columnar/dataframe pipelines. Not a fit here.
- **Reciprocal rank fusion.** Not a retriever -- a way to combine two you already have, in about fifteen lines of stdlib. See §3.

### Pure-Python / CPU packages

- **`bm25s`** -- the one to reach for if you want a BM25 *package*. It precomputes a sparse score matrix at index time, so a query is a matrix slice rather than a Python loop over posting lists. Supports BM25+/BM25L and the Lucene and Robertson variants, memory-maps its index, optional stemmer.
- **`rank_bm25`** -- the ubiquitous first hit. Simple API, but it iterates in Python over the whole corpus per query, so it degrades past small corpora. `src/retrieval.py`'s docstring is right that it isn't worth the dependency.
- **`tantivy`** (Python bindings to the Rust engine) -- Lucene-shaped: schemas, fielded queries, fast incremental indexing, BM25 default. The "I want a real search engine, not a scoring function, but not a server" option.
- **`whoosh-reloaded`** -- pure-Python Lucene-alike, maintained fork of Whoosh. Nice query parser, fine for modest corpora.

### Model-based, CPU-viable

- **Cross-encoder rerankers** -- `sentence-transformers`' `CrossEncoder` with a bge or mixedbread reranker; **`flashrank`** for tiny ONNX models with no torch dependency; Cohere/Voyage rerank if an API call is acceptable (it isn't here -- this repo is deliberately API-key-free). Highest quality per unit of effort on this whole list. See §3.

### Model-based, heavier

- **Dense bi-encoders** -- what `src/heavy/embed_index.py` already is.
- **SPLADE (learned sparse)** -- a model expands and weights terms, but the output is still a sparse vector in an inverted index. Much of the semantic benefit while staying interpretable. Via `pyserini` or HuggingFace.
- **ColBERT/PLAID**, most easily through **RAGatouille** -- late interaction, per-token embeddings. Strong quality, notably larger index.
- **PyTerrier** / **Pyserini** -- research-grade IR toolkits. The right choice for *evaluating* alternatives (nDCG/MRR against a judged set) rather than swapping one in. Both want a JVM, which is a heavier ask than anything currently in the `heavy` group.

### Servers and managed engines

OpenSearch/Elasticsearch (BM25 + kNN + RRF built in), Vespa, Qdrant/Weaviate/LanceDB with native hybrid. Worth it for multi-tenant serving and filtering at scale. Out of scope for a local corpus tool.

---

## 3. The hybrid pipeline, stage by stage

```
                    +--> BM25 / lexical -----> ranked list A --+
query --> analyze --|                                          |--> RRF --> cross-encoder --> top-k
                    +--> bi-encoder / dense -> ranked list B --+     fusion      rerank
```

### Stage 0 -- chunking and indexing (offline)

Sets the ceiling on every stage after it. Two decisions:

**The unit of retrieval.** Dense retrieval essentially forces chunking, because a bi-encoder compresses its input into one fixed-size vector and has a hard maximum sequence length -- feed it a twenty-page paper and everything past the limit is silently truncated, not summarised. Lexical retrieval has no such limit, which is why BM25 can score whole documents happily. This is the root of the granularity difference RETRIEVAL.md's table already records ("a whole document" vs "a 200-word chunk"), not an arbitrary choice on either side.

**Chunk boundaries.** Fixed word windows with overlap are the cheap default; the overlap exists so a sentence straddling a boundary still appears intact somewhere. Structure-aware chunking -- split on section headers, keep paragraphs whole, prepend the section title to each chunk -- is meaningfully better when the structure is available, because it stops a chunk from spanning two unrelated arguments.

### Stage 1a -- lexical retrieval (BM25)

Term overlap with two corrections: IDF (rare terms count more) and length normalisation with saturation. `k1` caps how much repeating a term helps; `b` interpolates between no length normalisation at all (`b = 0`) and full normalisation against the corpus *average* length (`b = 1`), so it boosts shorter-than-average documents as much as it penalises longer-than-average ones. RETRIEVAL.md records this repo's values (`k1 = 1.5`, `b = 0.75`), which are the usual defaults and are not tuned against this corpus.

Uniquely good at **exact tokens with no semantic neighbourhood**: citekeys, author surnames, `HDBSCAN`, `all-mpnet-base-v2`, error strings. An embedding of `all-mpnet-base-v2` sits right next to one of `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`; BM25 knows they are different strings.

Structurally cannot match "how do I keep the index from going stale" to a passage reading "incremental cache invalidation on fingerprint mismatch". No shared terms, no score.

### Stage 1b -- dense retrieval (bi-encoder)

Query and chunks pass through the *same* encoder, independently, into one vector each; retrieval is approximate nearest neighbour. "Independently" is the key word -- every chunk is encoded once, offline, and the query never influences that encoding. That is what makes it fast, and also what caps its quality: the model must decide what a chunk means before knowing what anyone will ask.

Two details that decide whether it works well:

- **Symmetric vs asymmetric.** Models trained on sentence similarity (the `all-*` family, including this repo's default) assume query and document look alike. A short question against a long passage is *asymmetric*; models trained for that (E5, BGE, GTE) expect a `query:`/`passage:` prefix and quietly underperform without it.
- **Normalisation and metric.** With unit-length vectors, cosine, dot product and Euclidean rank identically; without, they don't. Some sentence-transformers models include a normalisation layer, others require `normalize_embeddings=True`. A mismatch degrades ranking with no error.

### Stage 2 -- reciprocal rank fusion

The two lists have incomparable scores: BM25 emits an unbounded positive score, Chroma emits a distance where *lower* is better. Normalising them onto a common scale is fragile -- it is per-query, and one outlier rescales everything. RRF ignores scores and fuses **ranks**:

```python
def rrf(ranked_lists, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for lst in ranked_lists:                  # each: [id, id, ...] best-first
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(lst, 1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```

That is the entire algorithm. The `k` constant (60 is the conventional value from Cormack et al.) damps the top of each list, so an item ranked 3rd by *both* retrievers outranks one ranked 1st by only one. That behaviour is the point: agreement between independent methods is evidence.

No tuning, no per-query normalisation, no assumption that the two scales mean anything comparable. A weighted score blend can beat it *given labelled data to tune the weight* -- which this project does not have and would have to build.

Retrieve deeper than you need here (top ~50-100 per retriever); fusion only helps if the right item is somewhere in at least one list.

### Stage 3 -- cross-encoder reranking

The bi-encoder had to encode chunks before seeing the query. A cross-encoder does not: it takes `[query, chunk]` as one concatenated input and runs full attention across both, emitting a single relevance score. That is why it is more accurate, and why it can never be an index -- the score depends on the pair, so nothing precomputes. Cost is one forward pass per candidate, so it runs only on the ~50-100 survivors of fusion, never the corpus.

Sizes run from tiny ONNX models (`flashrank`, milliseconds on CPU) through `bge-reranker-base`/`mxbai-rerank` (a few hundred ms on CPU for ~50 candidates). Adding *just* this stage on top of plain BM25 is typically the single biggest win available.

### Stage 4 -- aggregate to the caller's unit

If you retrieved chunks but the caller wants documents, collapse: group surviving chunks by document, take max score (best single piece of evidence) or a decayed sum (rewards several good passages), then take top-k documents. Skipping this is a classic bug -- the caller asks for fifteen results, gets fifteen chunks from four papers, and concludes the corpus is thin.

### Cost shape

| Stage | Offline | Per query |
|---|---|---|
| Chunk + index | parse + one encode per chunk | -- |
| BM25 | inverted index build | sub-ms to low ms |
| Dense | ANN graph build | one query encode + ANN lookup |
| RRF | none | microseconds |
| Cross-encoder | none | N forward passes -- dominates |

---

## 4. How much of this already exists here

| Pipeline stage | chitragupta |
|---|---|
| Parse | `src/heavy/docling_parse.py` (layout-aware) or `pdftotext` -- **stronger than most projects' Stage 0** |
| Chunk | `embed_index.chunk_text()` -- 200-word windows, 40-word overlap |
| Dense index | `embed_index.build_index()` -> Chroma, namespaced per model |
| Lexical | `src/retrieval.py` -- hand-rolled Okapi BM25 |
| Fusion | absent, by design (RETRIEVAL.md) |
| Rerank | absent |
| Aggregate | n/a today, because nothing fuses |
| Topic clustering | `src/heavy/topic_model.py` -- *not a retrieval stage* |

Roughly two-thirds of the machinery is built. Four observations about the remaining third.

### 4.1 The either/or is a real design choice, and worth revisiting

`src/retrieval.py`'s docstring calls the embedding index a *replacement*: "swap in ... once BM25 stops being enough". The consistent finding in the IR literature is that lexical and dense errors are complementary -- they fail on disjoint inputs -- and fusing them beats either alone. That does not make the current choice wrong; it makes "which one do I build?" the wrong question to be forced into.

Concretely, on this corpus: BM25 wins on `assert_no_citekey_collision`, an author surname, or a specific model identifier. Dense wins on "papers arguing that co-simulation coupling is the bottleneck" when no paper uses that phrasing. A survey draft needs both, and today a skill picks one per session.

### 4.2 Granularity is the actual obstacle to fusing them

RETRIEVAL.md's table already records this ("a whole document" vs "a 200-word chunk"); it is worth naming as the concrete engineering blocker rather than a curiosity:

- `retrieval.search()` indexes one entry per citekey and returns `SearchResult(citekey, title, score, snippet)` -- a dataclass, higher is better. `k=5` means five distinct papers.
- `embed_index.search()` indexes one entry per chunk and returns `list[dict]` with `distance` -- lower is better. `k=5` means five chunks, possibly all from one paper.

So fusing needs a chunk-to-document collapse (Stage 4) before the ranks are over comparable items. RRF happens to make the polarity half free, since it never touches scores.

A related detail for anyone wiring this up in Python rather than through a skill: the "drop-in" property both docstrings advertise holds at the *signature*, not the return type. `r.citekey` vs `r["citekey"]`, `score` vs `distance`, different result cardinality. That is fine for the genre skills, which shell out and read printed output -- which is exactly how `deep-research` and `survey-writer` use it -- but a Python caller cannot alias one for the other.

### 4.3 Docling's structure survives into the text, but not into the chunk boundaries

RETRIEVAL.md is accurate that `--stages docling,embed` gives "better reading order in, better chunks out" -- `embed_index.get_text()` prefers `content/docling/<doc>.md`, and reading order genuinely matters given that 82-89% of long `pdftotext -layout` lines splice two columns together.

There is a further step available. `docling_parse._passage_records()` already writes `<stem>.passages.json` with, per prose item, its text, its label (`section_header`/`title`/`text`/`list_item`), its page number and its bounding box, with running heads and page numbers filtered out. `chunk_text()` then does `text.split()` on the flat markdown and slices every 160 words, so section and paragraph boundaries and page numbers are gone before anything is embedded. Only `src/citation_provenance.py` consumes the sidecar, via `src/passages.py`.

Chunking on `.passages.json` instead -- group consecutive prose items under their nearest `section_header`, prepend that header to each chunk, carry `page` into the Chroma metadata -- would improve embedding quality *and* let a retrieval hit report a page number. The data is already on disk and no new dependency is involved. This is a concrete shape for [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/prasadtalasila/chitragupta/blob/main/docs/DESIGN.md)'s recommendation 1, "use hierarchical document representations ... section-level text, page provenance".

### 4.4 BERTopic is orthogonal, and the docs already say so

Worth restating only because it shares a `--stages` list with the retrieval stages. BERTopic takes no query: embed each document whole, UMAP, HDBSCAN, c-TF-IDF labels. It answers a survey-structuring question. `topic_model.py`'s docstring and RETRIEVAL.md both already state that nothing reads `content/topics.json` and that all-outliers is a correct answer on a small corpus.

The one place it could touch retrieval is as a facet -- retrieve within a cluster when drafting a survey section on that theme. I would not build that until the corpus is large enough for HDBSCAN to produce non-outlier clusters at all.

### 4.5 What this stack already does better than the standard advice

The incremental-caching discipline is unusually thorough and is load-bearing for anything added later. `build_index()` stores a hash of the *text that produced the chunk*, not the PDF bytes, and deletes-then-reinserts on change so a shrinking chunk count cannot orphan trailing vectors. Chroma collections are namespaced per model, so changing `embedding_model` starts a clean collection instead of mixing dimensions. Most RAG codebases have both of those bugs.

---

## 5. Reference: how sentence-transformers is used today

*Reference material -- skip to §6 for the proposals, which don't depend on it.* Collected here because it is scattered across three modules and easy to get wrong from memory.

**Dependency status.** Declared in `pyproject.toml`'s optional `heavy` group (`sentence-transformers = ">=5.6,<6.0"`), installed only by `poetry install --with heavy` into `.venv-full`. Pulls `torch` transitively, which `scripts/install_full_pipeline.sh`'s `ensure_gpu_torch` then reinstalls from a CUDA-matched wheel index. Nothing in the corpus layer can import it.

**Model selection.** `config.EMBEDDING_MODEL`, default `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`. Note that `config.toml.example` ships a *different* value, `all-mpnet-base-v2` -- so a bare run and a run from the example config use different models and different vector dimensions. The per-model collection namespacing handles that correctly rather than corrupting the index.

**One construction site.** `embed_index.get_client_and_model()` is the only place `SentenceTransformer` is imported or instantiated in the repository. The import is inside the function, so importing `embed_index` does not drag in torch.

**Three call sites, two granularities:**

1. **Indexing** -- `build_index()`: `model.encode(chunks)` over 200-word chunks, upserted into Chroma with `doc_id`/`citekey`/`source`/`title`/`text_hash` metadata. Vectors are computed here and handed to Chroma explicitly, so no Chroma embedding function is registered -- sentence-transformers *is* the embedding function and Chroma is purely store plus ANN index.
2. **Query** -- `search()`: `model.encode([query])`, then `collection.query(query_embeddings=...)`. This reloads the model per call, which is fine for a skill shelling out once and wasteful in a loop.
3. **Topic modelling** -- `topic_model.run_topic_model()` calls `embed_index.get_client_and_model()` specifically to reuse the same model, encodes **whole documents** (not chunks), caches each vector as `{hash, model, embedding}` in `content/topic_embed_cache.json`, and passes both the model and the precomputed matrix to `BERTopic(embedding_model=model, ...)`. `topic_model.py`'s docstring is explicit that this cache is deliberately not shared with Chroma's -- per-chunk for retrieval, per-document for clustering, different granularity.

**Two things worth checking on this setup:**

- **Chunk size against the model's truncation limit.** 200 words is roughly 260-300 tokens, in the same range as these models' maximum sequence length. Anything past the limit is dropped silently, with no warning. Worth printing `model.max_seq_length` once and sizing chunks under it -- and re-checking after any `embedding_model` change, since the two configured models differ here.
- **Whole-document encoding in `topic_model.py`.** The same limit applies with far more force: a full paper encoded as one vector is truncated to its opening few hundred tokens, so clustering is effectively over each paper's abstract and introduction. That may well be *fine* -- abstracts are topically representative -- but it is currently implicit. Mean-pooling the document's chunk vectors (already in Chroma) would use the whole text. Given §4.4, this only matters if the topic model ever gets a consumer.

---

## 6. Proposals, in the order I would do them

1. **RRF fusion.** No new dependency, ~15 lines of stdlib, plus a chunk-to-document collapse for the dense side. Turns the current either/or into an upgrade path. Needs a decision on where it lives -- it cannot go in `src/retrieval.py` without the corpus layer gaining an optional dependency on the enrichment layer, and the dependency currently runs the other way everywhere.
2. **Passage-aware chunking.** No new dependency, uses `<stem>.passages.json` that is already written. Improves embedding quality and adds page numbers to hits, which is worth something on its own for `citation_provenance`.
3. **Cross-encoder reranking.** One new `heavy`-group dependency (`flashrank` for ONNX-only, or a `CrossEncoder` on the existing sentence-transformers). Largest per-query quality gain, largest per-query cost. This is DESIGN.md's recommendation 4, "BM25 or vector retrieval first, lightweight reranker second" -- §3 above is what the missing middle between those two lines looks like.
4. **SQLite FTS5 instead of the hand-rolled index.** Genuinely tempting -- it would delete the `retrieval_index.json` fingerprint cache and stay stdlib-only -- but the current cache works, and FTS5's compile-time-optional status means a fallback path anyway. Lowest priority of the four; listed because it is the only option that *reduces* code.

## 7. Open questions

- Is retrieval quality actually the binding constraint right now, or is corpus size? On a small, vocabulary-consistent corpus RETRIEVAL.md's "BM25 is usually enough" is probably right, and all of the above is premature.
- How would any of this be *evaluated*? None of it is worth merging on the strength of an argument. A small judged set -- twenty queries against this corpus with relevant citekeys marked by hand -- would make each proposal a measurement rather than a preference. That set is arguably the real prerequisite, and it is the cheapest item on this whole page.
- Does the layering permit fusion at all, or does hybrid search belong entirely in the enrichment layer with the corpus layer left untouched?

---

*Consolidated from a Claude Code session. Code references are against `main` at `d299eb4`; nothing here has been implemented or benchmarked.*

# Sprint Plan for AI-Native Autoscaling

## Phase 0: Workload Unification — Three-Level Canonical Model

**Goal:** Unify all workload generation through a single canonical spec format, retire legacy code paths, and set up the foundation for non-stationary workloads that autoscaling requires.

### Motivation

BLIS currently has three workload generation paths (CLI distribution-based, WorkloadSpec YAML, CSV trace replay) with ~300 lines of duplicated code across `sim/workload_config.go` and `sim/cluster/workload.go`. Features are scattered: rate stages are locked behind inference-perf, empirical PDFs behind ServeGen, multi-turn behind the reasoning block. These paths are mutually exclusive — you can't compose a ServeGen empirical distribution with inference-perf rate stages and multi-turn reasoning.

The unification introduces a **three-level canonical model** where every feature is composable, and external formats (ServeGen, inference-perf, GuideLLM, CSV traces) become **converters** that produce the canonical format.

### The Three-Level Model

```
Level 1: CLIENT POPULATION PROCESS — "Who is active, and when?"
│  Clients arrive and depart over time. Each client targets a specific model.
│  Non-stationary load is an emergent property of population dynamics:
│  diurnal = many arrivals at peak hours; spike = burst of arrivals;
│  scale-to-zero = all clients depart.
│
└─ Level 2: REQUEST GENERATION PROCESS — "How does this client produce requests?"
   │  Each active client generates requests at its own rate with its own
   │  token distributions, arrival process, prefix affinity, and modality.
   │
   └─ Level 3: CONVERSATION PROCESS — "How do turns within a request unfold?"
      Multi-turn sessions with think time, context accumulation,
      and reasoning token ratios.
```

### Canonical Spec Format (v2)

```yaml
version: "2"
seed: 42
horizon: 86400000000  # microseconds

# Level 1: Client population — two specification modes

# Mode A: Explicit clients with lifecycles (for controlled experiments, trace replay)
clients:
  - id: "web-user-1"
    model: "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct"
    arrives_at_us: 0
    departs_at_us: 43200000000
    request_process:              # Level 2
      arrival: {process: "poisson", rate: 2.0}
      input_distribution: {type: "gaussian", params: {mean: 256, std_dev: 100, min: 10, max: 2048}}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 128}}
      prefix_group: "system-prompt-v2"
      prefix_length: 256
      multimodal: ...             # optional
    conversation:                 # Level 3 (optional)
      multi_turn: {max_rounds: 3, think_time_us: 500000, context_growth: "accumulate"}
    slo_class: "interactive"
    streaming: true

# Mode B: Statistical cohorts (for generating realistic population dynamics)
cohorts:
  - name: "web-users"
    model: "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct"
    count: 200
    arrival_process: {type: "poisson", rate: 50.0}  # client arrival rate
    session_duration: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 1800000000}}  # ~30min
    diurnal:
      peak_hour: 14
      trough_hour: 4
      peak_trough_ratio: 5.0
    request_process:
      arrival: {process: "poisson", rate: 0.5}
      input_distribution: {type: "gaussian", params: {mean: 256, std_dev: 100, min: 10, max: 2048}}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 128}}
    conversation:
      multi_turn: {max_rounds: 5, think_time_us: 500000, context_growth: "accumulate"}
    slo_class: "realtime"

  - name: "batch-jobs"
    model: "qwen/qwen-2.5-7b"
    count: 10
    arrival_process: {type: "constant", rate: 0.001}
    session_duration: {type: "constant", params: {value: 86400000000}}
    request_process:
      arrival: {process: "gamma", cv: 3.5, rate: 20.0}
      input_distribution: {type: "empirical", file: "production_input_pdf.json"}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 512}}
```

### Converter Architecture

The simulator only parses the canonical format. External formats are supported through converters that produce canonical YAML:

```
  blis convert servegen ──────┐
  blis convert inference-perf ┼──► Canonical YAML ──► Simulator
  blis convert preset ────────┤    (one format)       (one parser)
  blis convert csv-trace ─────┤
  hand-written YAML ──────────┘
```

```bash
# Convert ServeGen traces → canonical spec
blis convert servegen /data/production/ -o workload.yaml

# Convert inference-perf config → canonical spec
blis convert inference-perf config.yaml -o workload.yaml

# Convert GuideLLM preset → canonical spec
blis convert preset chatbot --rate 100 --num-requests 500 -o workload.yaml

# Convert legacy CSV traces → canonical spec
blis convert csv-trace traces.csv -o workload.yaml

# Compose multiple sources (convenience helper)
blis compose \
  --from-servegen /data/production/:0.5 \
  --from-preset chatbot:0.3 \
  --from-spec spike-test.yaml:0.2 \
  -o combined.yaml
```

Composition happens at the YAML level — merge client/cohort lists, adjust rate fractions. Adding support for a new external format tomorrow is just a new `blis convert <format>` subcommand with zero changes to the spec or simulator.

### Supported Features (all composable on any client)

| Feature | Level | Available on any client |
|---------|-------|------------------------|
| Arrival process (Poisson, Gamma, Weibull, Constant) | 2 | Yes |
| Token distributions (Gaussian, Exponential, ParetoLogNormal, Empirical, Constant) | 2 | Yes |
| Multimodal (text, image, audio, video) | 2 | Yes |
| Prefix groups + prefix length | 2 | Yes |
| Multi-turn reasoning with context accumulation | 3 | Yes |
| SLO class / tenant ID | Client | Yes |
| Streaming mode | Client | Yes |
| Network model (RTT + bandwidth) | Client | Yes |
| Model affinity | Client | Yes |
| Client lifecycle (arrives/departs) | 1 | Yes |
| Diurnal population dynamics | 1 (cohorts) | Yes |
| Session duration distribution | 1 (cohorts) | Yes |

### What Gets Retired

- `GuideLLMConfig` struct and its 11-parameter constructor
- `sim/workload_config.go` — entire file (~170 lines of duplicated generation/CSV parsing)
- `sim/cluster/workload.go` — `generateRequestsFromDistribution()` and `generateRequestsFromCSV()` (~100 lines)
- The 4-way `if/else` in `cmd/root.go` for workload selection
- The placeholder `GuideLLMConfig` hack when using WorkloadSpec

### What Gets Added

- `"constant"` arrival process (deterministic fixed-rate, for GuideLLM backward compatibility)
- `model` field on clients (for multi-model autoscaling)
- `cohorts` specification mode (statistical population dynamics)
- `blis convert` subcommands (servegen, inference-perf, preset, csv-trace)
- `blis compose` convenience helper
- v1 → v2 spec migration (v1 specs still parse, auto-promoted internally)

### CLI Backward Compatibility

Existing CLI invocations continue to work — they internally synthesize a canonical spec:

| CLI Command | Internal Translation |
|-------------|---------------------|
| `blis run --rate 100 --prompt-tokens 512` | Single client, constant arrival, Gaussian distributions |
| `blis run --workload chatbot` | Single client from preset template |
| `blis run --workload traces --workload-traces-filepath X` | Explicit clients from CSV |
| `blis run --workload-spec X.yaml` | Direct parse (v1 or v2) |

***

## Phase 1A: Foundation — Make BLIS Dynamically Scalable

**Goal:** Extend the DES kernel so instances can be added/removed mid-simulation.

### Architecture Prerequisites
- [ ] Design doc: Instance lifecycle abstraction (`AddInstance`/`RemoveInstance` on `ClusterSimulator`)
  - Resolve fixed `[]*InstanceSimulator` slice → ID-indexed map or dynamic slice
  - `CachedSnapshotProvider` must handle instance arrival/departure
  - `pendingRequests` bookkeeping already uses string keys (robust)
  - Define instance states: `Provisioning → WarmingUp → Active → Draining → Terminated`
  - Scale-to-zero: relax `NumInstances >= 1` panic; define "cold start from zero" event sequence
- [ ] Design doc: Heterogeneous instance configuration
  - Per-instance `SimConfig` (different model, GPU, TP config per instance)
  - Extend `DeploymentConfig` → `[]InstanceConfig` or multiple `DeploymentConfig` objects
  - Routing implications: scorer weights may differ per-model (e.g., prefix-affinity irrelevant for some models)
  - Model-aware routing: requests with `model` field routed only to instances serving that model

### Core Autoscaler Module
- [ ] Design doc: Autoscaler subsystem module (per design guidelines §5.3)
  - Module contract: observes (metrics, queue depth, KV utilization), controls (instance count), owns (scaling state, cooldown timers), invariants (min ≤ replicas ≤ max, no scale during cooldown)
  - Event types: `AutoScaleCheckEvent`, `ScaleActionEvent`, `InstanceReadyEvent` (priority after routing/step/completion)
  - `AutoScalePolicy` interface (single-method: `Decide(AutoScaleContext) ScaleDecision`)
  - Strawman policies: `ThresholdScaler` (reactive), `PredictiveScaler` (trend-based), `Oscillator` (pathological control)
  - Actuation model: `ProvisioningDelay` (distribution), `WarmupProfile` (duration, cache cold-start penalty), `DrainPolicy` (immediate/wait/redirect)
  - Scale-to-zero: `DrainPolicy.DRAIN_ALL` + `MinReplicas=0`; cold-start-from-zero latency model
- [ ] Derive invariants:
  - INV-A1: `active_instances + provisioning_instances + draining_instances = total_managed_instances`
  - INV-A2: No routing to `Provisioning` or `Draining` instances
  - INV-A3: Scale-down must drain queue before terminating (or redirect in-flight)
- [ ] Derive hypotheses (pre-implementation, to validate post-implementation):
  - H-ScaleUp: Adding instance at ρ>0.8 reduces TTFT p99 by >30% within 2× provisioning_delay
  - H-ScaleDown: Removing instance at ρ<0.3 has <5% TTFT impact (headroom absorbs)
  - H-Oscillation: Naive threshold scaler with tight bounds produces scale oscillation (>3 scale events per 10× service_time)
  - H-WarmupCost: Cold instance with empty KV cache has >2× TTFT vs warm instance for first N requests
  - H-ScaleToZero: Cold-start-from-zero adds provisioning_delay + warmup_time to first request E2E
  - H-MultiModel: Model-aware routing with heterogeneous instances matches homogeneous per-model clusters within 10% TTFT

### Metrics & Observability Extensions
- [ ] New metrics: scaling_events_count, provisioning_latency_p99, instances_active (time-series), cost_proxy (instance-seconds), SLO_violation_rate
- [ ] Extend `ComputeFitness()` with cost and scaling-efficiency dimensions
- [ ] Extend counterfactual analysis: "what if we had scaled 30s earlier?"
- [ ] Trace records: `ScaleRecord` (already templated in extension-recipes.md)

### Macro Plan Derivation
- [ ] Derive PR sequence from the above design docs. Likely structure:
  - PR-W1: Workload unification — canonical spec v2, retire legacy paths, converters
  - PR-W2: Cohort-based population dynamics (non-stationary workloads)
  - PR-A1: Instance lifecycle (AddInstance/RemoveInstance + states + tests)
  - PR-A2: Autoscaler core (interface + ThresholdScaler + events + metrics)
  - PR-A3: Actuation model (provisioning delay, warmup, drain)
  - PR-A4: Heterogeneous instances + multi-model routing
  - PR-A5: Scale-to-zero support
  - PR-A6: Hypothesis experiments (H-ScaleUp through H-ScaleToZero)
- [ ] Validate llm-d/WVA alignment at each PR boundary
  - WPA (Workload-Proportional Autoscaling) maps to ThresholdScaler with utilization target
  - EPP (Endpoint Picker Policy) maps to existing composable scorer framework
  - Model routing maps to PR-A4 multi-model extension

***

## Phase 1B: Implementation Sprint

**Goal:** Land all PRs on an `autoscaling` feature branch.

- [ ] For each PR in the macro plan:
  - Run the PR workflow (micro-plan → convergence review → implement → code review → self-audit)
  - **Keep automated convergence rounds** (10 perspectives) — these catch real bugs every time
  - Skip the human gate at Step 3 (plan approval) for velocity — human reviews at branch merge instead
  - Merge into `autoscaling` branch (not `main`)
- [ ] Run hypothesis experiments (PR-A6) to validate autoscaler behavior
- [ ] Rebase `autoscaling` on `upstream/main`, resolve conflicts
- [ ] Full human review of the consolidated branch
- [ ] Merge into `main`

***

## Phase 1C: Evolutionary Algorithm Discovery

**Goal:** Use LLM-guided evolution to discover autoscaling algorithms that outperform hand-designed policies.

### Fitness Function Design
- [ ] Define the multi-objective fitness landscape:
  - **Latency**: TTFT p99, E2E p99 (from existing `ComputeFitness`)
  - **Cost**: total instance-seconds (minimize)
  - **SLO compliance**: fraction of requests meeting SLO target
  - **Stability**: scaling event frequency (penalize oscillation)
  - **Responsiveness**: time from overload detection to scale-up completion
- [ ] Define behavioral feature dimensions for MAP-Elites ([OpenEvolve](https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve)):
  - Workload regime (steady/bursty/diurnal)
  - Scale range (2-4 instances vs 4-16 vs 16-64)
  - Model mix (single-model vs multi-model)

### OpenEvolve Integration — Algorithm Structure Discovery
- [ ] Design the evolvable program template:
  - The `AutoScalePolicy.Decide()` method body is the evolved code
  - `AutoScaleContext` (signals) is the fixed input interface
  - `ScaleDecision` is the fixed output interface
  - BLIS simulation is the fitness evaluator (deterministic, fast, no GPU needed)
- [ ] Configure OpenEvolve:
  - Sandbox: BLIS binary execution (CPU-only, ~seconds per evaluation)
  - Evaluation suite: N workload scenarios (steady, burst, diurnal, spike, scale-to-zero recovery)
  - Seeds: multiple seeds per scenario for determinism validation (INV-6)
  - Quality-diversity: MAP-Elites over (workload_regime × scale_range) feature space
- [ ] Run evolution campaigns, collect Pareto-optimal algorithm set

### GEPA Integration — Parameter Tuning
- [ ] Implement `GEPAAdapter` for BLIS:
  - `evaluate()`: run BLIS with candidate policy, return multi-objective scores
  - `make_reflective_dataset()`: extract execution traces (scaling events, queue depth time-series, SLO violations) as Actionable Side Information
- [ ] For each promising algorithm from OpenEvolve:
  - Use [GEPA](https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa) to tune thresholds, cooldown periods, look-back windows
  - GEPA's trace reflection identifies *why* specific scaling decisions were suboptimal
  - ~100-500 evaluations per algorithm (vs thousands for RL)

### Landing Results
- [ ] Select best candidates (Pareto-optimal across cost/latency/stability)
- [ ] Add as named `AutoScalePolicy` implementations (e.g., `EvolvedReactiveScaler`, `EvolvedPredictiveScaler`)
- [ ] Merge into `autoscaling` branch with hypothesis validation
- [ ] Rebase, resolve conflicts, full review, merge into `main`

***

## Phase 2: Sim-to-Real Transfer

**Goal:** Bridge BLIS-evolved algorithms to production llm-d deployments.

_Expand after Phase 1 experience. Likely topics:_

- [ ] Calibration pipeline: real cluster telemetry → BLIS coefficient fitting (alpha/beta per model/GPU)
- [ ] Policy export format: BLIS `AutoScalePolicy` → llm-d WPA controller config
- [ ] Online adaptation: GEPA reflective loop on production traces (not just sim traces)
- [ ] Validation protocol: shadow-mode comparison (BLIS prediction vs real scaling decisions)
- [ ] Feedback loop: production anomalies → new BLIS hypothesis experiments → algorithm refinement

nodes.title: Saturation detection across the LLM inference stack: where it is used, where it could be used, and what signals are available
